extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; media professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of how organizational routines, roles, ownership, and economic goals shape news production and content; used for analyzing media organizations and news output. Emphasizes organization-level gatekeeping, economic constraints, and role-based perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routines shape news content
rubrics_metrics.description: Routines have an important impact on the production of symbolic content; they form the immediate environment within which individual media workers carry out their jobs and constrain the individual while also arising from external constraints (audience time/attention, organizational resources, source limitations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: event focus aids scheduling and provides a concrete focus for audiences; routines provide levers that outside power centers can grasp to influence content; routines are interconnected and cannot be separated from organizational or source constraints. Use this criterion to assess whether routine-driven structures (event focus, beat systems, scheduling) are evident and how they limit alternative perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on sources leads to compliance and co-optation
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong dependence of journalists on sources (e.g., the military) can produce co-optation, leading to uncritical acceptance of source frames of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs include reporters adopting source language and identifications ('we invaded', 'our troops'), regular use of former officials or source-affiliated 'experts' who identify with official policy, and examples like pool journalists treated as 'their' journalists. Use this to evaluate whether coverage reflects source-defined success criteria rather than independent criteria (diplomatic, economic, moral, environmental).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical alignment (use of 'we'/'our') indicates co-optation
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of inclusive language such as 'we' and 'our' in news discourse rhetorically binds reporters (and audiences) to governmental or military interests, signifying co-optation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detectable in anchors' and reporters' phrasing (e.g., 'We invaded,' 'our troops,' 'our country') and in hiring/former military experts who identify with policy. Use as a linguistic indicator of lack of critical distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competitive access can make journalists protect exclusives and increase dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once journalists are granted access to pools of information, competitive pressures can make them more concerned with protecting exclusive rights to news than with ensuring reasonable access for other journalists; paradoxically this increases compliance and dependence on sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ottosen quote: reporters protect exclusive front access; this criterion evaluates how competitive access arrangements (pools, exclusives) affect newsroom independence and whether they produce protective behavior that aligns journalists with sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization as the gatekeeper (collective, hierarchical decision-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: News selection and 'gatekeeping' should be viewed as a complex, organization-wide process rather than the action of isolated individual gatekeepers; the organization as a whole functions as the gatekeeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the NBC Loan film example: multiple levels (Saigon crew, bureau chief, Tokyo producer, New York executive producer) participated in the decision; time pressures and organizational norms influenced edits. Evaluate decisions for evidence of multi-level organizational involvement and collective deliberation rather than single-person choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational roles and hierarchy shape perspectives and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Different organizational roles (front-line reporters, middle managers/editors/producers, top corporate/news executives) have distinct duties, authorities, and vantage points that affect views and decisions about content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess recruitment paths (e.g., television management coming from sales), the differing agendas of editors versus reporters (editors more audience-related; reporters more source-related), and how role power and specialization influence content decisions, bargaining, and compliance with higher-level policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key organization-chart questions for evaluating influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Four basic analytic questions: (1) What are the organizational roles? (2) How is the organization structured? (3) What is the policy and how is it implemented? (4) How are these policies enforced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these questions to map who does what, the lines of authority (centralized vs decentralized), the content of policies transmitted through the structure, and mechanisms of enforcement. Use to diagnose structural causes of content variation and the formal/informal strength of authority lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational policies from the top can override lower-level routines
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific policies issued from organizational leaders can overrule lower-level routines and individual practices; organizational leaders make and enforce policy on behalf of the organization in service of organization-level goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate instances where top-down policies constrain reporter routines (e.g., editorial directives, resource allocations) and consider how policy enforcement mechanisms (promotion, firing, budget control) change news content outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ownership and interlocks influence content
rubrics_metrics.description: Who owns the media organization (including nonmedia owners and interlocking corporate interests) affects content because corporate goals and relationships permeate the firm and shape priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: corporate parents (Loews-CBS, GE-NBC), shared board memberships, cross-ownership, major advertisers/stockholders (Capital Cities/ABC and RJR Nabisco). Use this to assess whether ownership ties, cross-industry investments, or board interlocks create incentives that bias coverage or create conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of economic goals (profit motive)
rubrics_metrics.description: For most media organizations the primary goal is economic (profit); other goals like quality, public service, and professional recognition are secondary and must align with economic survival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether editorial choices are justified or constrained by profitability concerns, shareholder pressures, or corporate survival. Exceptions occur (owners prioritizing influence over profit), but generally use this to test whether economic imperatives shape content and priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic considerations function as constraints versus dictates
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic factors can act as constraints setting the parameters within which professional objectives operate (Sigal/Gans view), but in tighter financial conditions they become dictates that directly determine content and resource allocation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the financial health context: when revenues sufficed, professional goals often prevailed; with greater profit pressure, cost-cutting, bureau closures, and programming choices reflect economics as direct dictates. Use this to determine where a given organization falls on the constraint–dictate spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising-driven audience delivery (economic logic) shapes content
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial mass media earn revenue by delivering audiences to advertisers; audience desirability and compatibility with ads influence what content is produced and how much news 'space' is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include reduced news hole when ad lineage drops, programming trade-offs in television due to fixed time, and the tendency of newsmagazines and prime-time features to incorporate entertainment elements (celebrities, sex, crime) to attract desirable audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-cutting adaptations change formats and reduce depth
rubrics_metrics.description: When organizations reduce budgets they adopt practices (planning farther in advance, more picture stories, canned packaged stories, reruns, features replacing reporter packages) that lower production costs but can reduce depth and quality of journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use KTVY/KGO examples: increased prepackaged 'pseudo-events,' reliance on meteorologists for features, fewer follow-ups, fewer documentaries. Evaluate whether cost-saving measures have become entrenched efficiencies even after revenues improve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional economic base influences framing, sourcing, and coverage balance
rubrics_metrics.description: The local/regional economic base of a news organization (e.g., tobacco-growing regions) can produce a shading of content—differences in headlines, source selection, and event prominence that favor local economic interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Swisher & Reese analysis showed tobacco-region newspapers framed the EPA/Burns story more favorably to industry, used the Tobacco Institute more, and gave less coverage to anti-tobacco events. Use content comparisons across regions to detect economic shading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal role conflicts require mediation and affect content priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Different internal routines and role requirements (e.g., editors vs reporters) may bring them into conflict over resource allocation, coverage priorities, and beat structures; organizational mediation (requests, rotations, subordinating routines) resolves these but shapes content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: editors may favor audience-related priorities while reporters are source-related; editors can request rotations or restrict conformity to source-promoted ground rules. Assess how such mediation is implemented and its effect on editorial independence and coverage diversity.
